items.title: 8.15 Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium

blocks.text: A catalyst is that substance which increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself being consumed in the reaction. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position and the equilibrium constant of a chemical reaction. It speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is attained. It means that the yield of the chemical reaction remains the same.

A catalyst provides new path of lower activation energy for a reaction. If we plot a graph between reaction coordinate on x-axis and potential energy of the chemical reaction on y-axis, then the maxima of the curve become lower in the presence of a catalyst as shown in Figure 8.3.

blocks.alt: Energy (y) against reaction coordinate (x). Two humped curves start at the reactant level and end at the lower product level. The taller curve (uncatalyzed) and the lower curve (catalyzed) each peak at an activated state. A double arrow Ea (uncatalyzed reaction) runs from the reactant level to the upper peak, a double arrow E'a (catalyzed reaction) from the reactant level to the lower peak, and ΔH between the reactant and product levels.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.3: Effect of a catalyst on Reversible Reactions (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.3).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 8.3 runs the Ea (uncatalyzed reaction) arrow down to the products line. Activation energy is measured from the reactant level up to the top of the curve, as drawn above.
